analysis.one_liner: Froze large agribusiness mergers for up to 18 months and created a commission to study farm-market concentration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 1999 and died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped large agribusiness companies — big meatpackers, grain processors, seed and chemical suppliers, and dealers — from buying or merging with each other for up to 18 months, with waivers only for companies in financial distress. It also would have created a 12-member commission to study how much a handful of firms control farm markets and recommend changes to antitrust law. The stated aim was to slow the wave of consolidation that had left a few corporations controlling most pork, beef, soybean, and grain processing.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers, who would face more buyers competing for their crops and livestock, plus rural communities dependent on farm income and shoppers who the bill's findings say have not seen savings from low farm prices passed on at the supermarket.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, rural towns, and food shoppers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have frozen mergers among large agribusiness firms for 18 months or until Congress passed broader concentration legislation, whichever came first, with Attorney General waivers only for extraordinary circumstances like insolvency [S3].

The bill's findings state that the top four beef packers grew from 32% to 80% market share, top four pork packers from 36% to 57%, and top four soybean crushers from 54% to 80% in about fifteen years, and that the farmer's share of the retail food dollar fell from around 50% to under 25% [S3].

The bill would have created a commission to study concentration's effects on farmer income, rural communities, the environment, and food shoppers, including why Depression-level farm prices did not produce corresponding supermarket price drops, and to recommend antitrust changes [S3].

The bill's findings state that from 1984 to 1998 prices paid to farmers fell 36% while consumer food prices rose 3%, and that consolidation is driving family farmers out of business and hollowing out rural economies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness — meatpackers, grain processors, seed and chemical companies, and commodity dealers — would have been barred from acquisitions above the bill's size thresholds for the moratorium period, and the industry would have faced a formal study of its market power with an eye toward new antitrust rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large agribusiness processors, packers, and input suppliers.

drawbacks.text: A flat 18-month freeze on all large agribusiness acquisitions would have blocked some mergers even where competition would not be harmed; the bill's only escape valve was an Attorney General waiver for extraordinary circumstances such as insolvency [S3].
The bill directed appropriations of $2,000,000 for the new commission and left any real remedy to future legislation, so its direct benefits depended entirely on Congress acting again afterward [S3].

A moratorium treats consolidation as a whole as the problem, but some acquisitions involve genuinely distressed sellers; supporters acknowledged this by building the insolvency waiver, yet the freeze could still have paused efficiencies as well as concentration [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but narrow: 18 months without large agribusiness mergers, at the cost of freezing some deals that might have been harmless or even saved failing firms. The bill's lasting value would have come from the study commission and whatever legislation followed, not the moratorium itself. As a first step against documented concentration — four beef packers at 80% of the market, farmers getting under 25 cents of the retail food dollar — the design was defensible; its weakness was that nothing in it directly restored competition, it only bought time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 1999, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on October 15, 1999, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Senators Dorgan, Daschle, Feingold, Harkin, Johnson, and Leahy [S1] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any House action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large agribusiness firms were better off: no moratorium ever took effect, so meatpackers, grain processors, and farm-input companies could continue acquiring rivals while Congress studied nothing. Family farmers and rural communities got no relief from the consolidation documented in the bill's own findings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large agribusiness, which kept consolidating unchecked.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remaining 14-plus months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a recorded vote [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have barred firms with over $100 million in sales or assets from merging with or acquiring other large agribusiness firms for up to 18 months, directly blocking further consolidation by the top four beef, pork, and soybean processors. Their interest in continuing to acquire rivals ran against farmers seeking more buyers for their crops and livestock.

Input suppliers above the bill's size thresholds were covered by the merger moratorium, halting acquisitions in the seed, chemical, and fertilizer markets. Farmers buying these inputs would have benefited from less consolidation among their suppliers.

With a handful of firms controlling most processing of every major commodity, farmers' bargaining power has collapsed — the bill found the farm share of the retail food dollar fell below 25%. A merger freeze and a formal study of market power would have given small producers their best shot at more competing buyers and fairer prices.
